tagline: A prisoner's letter of thanks and joy to his most faithful church, centered on the Christ who emptied himself and was exalted.
overview:
Philippians is Paul's warmest letter. He writes from prison, facing a trial that could end in his death, to a church that had supported him from the beginning and had just sent him a gift by the hand of one of their own members, Epaphroditus. He thanks them, tells them how his imprisonment has actually spread the gospel, and urges them to stand together, to put others' interests ahead of their own, and to keep rejoicing in the Lord whatever their circumstances.

At the heart of the letter stands a passage many scholars think was an early Christian hymn (2:6-11). It tells how Christ Jesus, existing in the form of God, did not hold on to his equality with God but emptied himself, took the form of a servant, became human, and was obedient to death on a cross, and how God therefore exalted him and gave him the name above every name. Paul holds this up as the pattern of the mind believers are to share. The rest of the letter echoes it: Timothy and Epaphroditus are commended because they live this way, and Paul describes counting his own impressive credentials as loss for the sake of knowing Christ (3:4-11).

The letter is short, personal, and practical, and it contains some of the most loved lines in the New Testament: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21), “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!” (4:4), and “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength” (4:13), which in context is a statement about contentment in hunger and plenty.
author:
Paul wrote Philippians, with Timothy named alongside him in the greeting (1:1). This is one of the letters nearly all scholars, critical and traditional alike, accept as Paul's own. The personal details, the style, and the theology all fit him, and the letter was known and valued by the early church; Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna in the early second century, wrote his own letter to the Philippians and mentions that Paul had written to them.

The main debate concerns the letter's unity rather than its author. At 3:1 Paul writes “Finally, my brothers”, and at 3:2 the tone turns sharply to warning against opponents, which leads some scholars to think Philippians combines two or three shorter letters of Paul, perhaps including a separate note of thanks for the gift (4:10-20). Many others argue the letter is a single whole, pointing to shared vocabulary and themes that run through every section and noting that Paul often uses “finally” to mark a turn rather than an ending.
date: The date depends on where Paul was imprisoned, and there are three main views. The traditional view places him in Rome, under the house arrest described in Acts 28, around AD 60 to 62. The mention of the palace guard (the praetorium, 1:13) and of believers in the household of Caesar (4:22) fits Rome naturally, and Paul's uncertainty about whether he will live or die fits a trial before the emperor. A second view places him in Ephesus around AD 54 to 55. Acts does not record an imprisonment there, but Paul speaks of many imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:23) and of great danger in Asia, and Ephesus is much closer to Philippi, which would make the several trips implied in the letter (news of Paul's imprisonment, Epaphroditus's arrival, news of his illness reaching home, and his planned return) easier to explain. A third view places him in Caesarea, where he was held for two years around AD 57 to 59 in Herod's praetorium (Acts 23:35). Each has defenders; the Roman setting remains the most widely held, and the letter's message is the same on any of them.
setting:
Philippi lay in Macedonia, in what is now northern Greece, on the Via Egnatia, the Roman road that ran across the Balkans. It was founded in the fourth century BC by Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great, and named after him. In 42 BC, on the plain outside the city, Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, the assassins of Julius Caesar. Afterward, and again after Octavian's victory at Actium in 31 BC, the city was refounded as a Roman colony and settled with veterans of the Roman army.

As a colony, Philippi was a small piece of Rome planted abroad. Its citizens held Roman citizenship, it was governed by Roman law and Roman magistrates, Latin was prominent in its official life, and its people were proud of their status. That background gives force to Paul's language: he tells the believers to conduct themselves (literally, to live as citizens) in a manner worthy of the gospel (1:27), and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven (3:20). Acts 16 describes the founding of the church around AD 49 to 50 on Paul's second missionary trip: the conversion of Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, at a place of prayer by the river; the freeing of a slave girl from a spirit of divination; the beating and imprisonment of Paul and Silas; and the conversion of the jailer and his household. The church that began there went on to support Paul financially again and again (4:15-16), and faced opposition of its own (1:28-30).
purpose: Paul writes for several reasons at once. He thanks the Philippians for their gift and their long partnership in the gospel (1:3-5; 4:10-20). He reports on his circumstances and reassures them that his chains have advanced the gospel (1:12-26). He sends Epaphroditus home after a near-fatal illness, explaining why and asking the church to honor him (2:25-30), and plans to send Timothy soon (2:19-24). He urges unity and humility in a church where some members, including two women who had labored with him, Euodia and Syntyche, were at odds (2:1-4; 4:2-3). And he warns them against teachers who would put confidence in circumcision and the flesh, and against those who live as enemies of the cross (3:2-21).
story: Philippians belongs to the period after Acts 16 to 20, when Paul's churches in Macedonia and Greece were growing and he himself was increasingly in chains. It is one of the four Prison Letters, alongside Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon. In the larger story of the Bible it shows the gospel reaching Europe and a Roman colony, and it shows a church learning to live as citizens of heaven while still inside the empire. Its central hymn draws on Isaiah's picture of every knee bowing to the Lord (Isaiah 45:23) and on the servant of the Lord who is humbled and then exalted, and it looks forward to the day of Christ, when the Savior will come from heaven and transform the bodies of his people (3:20-21).
christ: Philippians contains one of the most important statements about Christ in the New Testament. In 2:6-11, Christ Jesus exists in the form of God and has equality with God, yet he empties himself by taking the form of a servant and being made in human likeness, humbles himself to death on a cross, and is exalted by God and given the name above all names, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. The church's confession that Christ is truly God and truly human, and that he came down to save and was raised and exalted, is written plainly here. Christ is also the one Paul lives for (1:21), the one whose righteousness he receives by faith (3:9), whose sufferings and resurrection he wants to share (3:10), and whose return he awaits (3:20-21).
reading: Read Philippians as a real letter between friends, full of thanks, news, and practical requests. Watch for its key words: joy and rejoicing, the gospel, partnership (koinonia), mind or attitude (the same verb recurs through the letter), and the day of Christ. Notice how the Christ hymn in chapter 2 shapes what follows: Timothy, Epaphroditus, and Paul himself are all shown living out its pattern. Joy in this letter is not cheerfulness or denial; it sits beside chains, rivalry, illness, and the possibility of death. A common misreading lifts single verses such as 4:13 out of context and turns them into promises of success; in context they describe the strength to be content in need as well as in plenty.

structure.title: Greeting, thanks, and prayer
structure.summary: Paul greets the church, thanks God for their partnership in the gospel, and prays that their love will grow in knowledge and discernment.

structure.title: Paul's circumstances
structure.summary: His imprisonment has advanced the gospel; he rejoices that Christ is preached and weighs life and death, confident he will remain for their sake.

structure.title: A life worthy of the gospel
structure.summary: Stand firm together, look to others' interests, and share the mind of Christ, who emptied himself and was exalted; work out salvation and shine as lights.

structure.title: Timothy and Epaphroditus
structure.summary: Paul plans to send Timothy and sends Epaphroditus home, commending both as examples of self-giving service.

structure.title: Knowing Christ
structure.summary: Paul warns against confidence in the flesh, counts his credentials as loss to gain Christ, presses on toward the goal, and points to citizenship in heaven.

structure.title: Final appeals and thanks
structure.summary: Paul urges unity, joy, prayer instead of anxiety, and right thinking, thanks the church for its gift, and closes with greetings.

themes.title: Joy
themes.body: Words for joy and rejoicing appear more than a dozen times in this short letter, written by a man in chains. Paul's joy rests not on circumstances but on the Lord, on the progress of the gospel, and on his friendship with the Philippians. He rejoices that Christ is preached even by rivals (1:18), and he calls the church to rejoice in the Lord always (4:4). This is joy that has looked at suffering and death and not been undone by them.

themes.title: The mind of Christ
themes.body: The letter repeatedly uses a Greek verb meaning to think, to set one's mind, or to hold an attitude. Paul asks the church to be like-minded (2:2) and to have among themselves the mind that was in Christ Jesus (2:5), who did not grasp his status but emptied himself for others. Humility here is not low self-esteem but the free choice to use one's position for the good of others, as Christ did.

themes.title: Partnership in the gospel
themes.body: Paul thanks the Philippians for their partnership (koinonia, a word for shared life and common cause) from the first day (1:5). They prayed, they gave, and they sent one of their own to serve him. Philippians shows the Christian life as shared work in a common mission, not a private spirituality.

themes.title: Citizenship and conduct
themes.body: In a Roman colony proud of its citizenship, Paul tells believers to live as citizens worthy of the gospel (1:27) and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven (3:20). Their primary loyalty lies with the Lord Jesus Christ, whose coming they await, and that loyalty shapes how they live in Philippi.

themes.title: Suffering and hope
themes.body: Paul writes from prison, the church faces opposition, and Epaphroditus nearly died. The letter does not hide any of this. It sees suffering for Christ as a gift granted to believers (1:29), a sharing in Christ's sufferings (3:10), and it sets all of it within the hope of resurrection and the day of Christ.

keyChapters.why: Paul's thanksgiving and prayer, his report that chains have advanced the gospel, and his reflection that to live is Christ and to die is gain.
The Christ hymn (2:6-11), one of the central passages of the New Testament on who Christ is, set within a call to humility and unity.
Paul counts his own righteousness as loss in order to gain Christ and the righteousness that comes from God through faith.
Calls to rejoice, to pray instead of worrying, and to learn contentment, with Paul's thanks for the church's gift.

parts.body:
Philippians is a letter from Paul, written in prison, to the church in Philippi, a Roman city in northern Greece. It has 4 chapters and can be read aloud in about fifteen minutes.

It is the warmest letter Paul wrote. The church in Philippi was the first he planted in Europe, and it had stood by him from the start, praying for him, sending money again and again, and at last sending one of its own members, Epaphroditus, to look after him in prison. Paul writes to say thank you, to tell them how he is, and to help them with troubles of their own.

The surprising thing about the letter is its joy. Paul is in chains. He does not know whether he will be set free or put to death. Some other preachers are using his absence to make a name for themselves. His helper nearly died. And still the words for joy and rejoicing come again and again. “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!” (4:4).

At the heart of the letter is a song about Jesus (2:6-11). He shared God's own nature, yet he did not cling to his rights. He came down, became a man, became a servant, and went all the way to death on a cross. And God raised him to the highest place, so that one day every knee will bow to him. Paul asks his friends to have the same mind: to look not only to their own interests, but also to the interests of others.

The letter is short and personal, and it holds some of the most loved lines in the Bible: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21), and “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength” (4:13). Read in its place, that second line is about being content in hunger and in plenty. It is the strength of a prisoner, not a promise of success.

The letter opens, “Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus” (1:1). Timothy was with Paul and is named beside him, but Paul speaks in his own voice all through, and he speaks of Timothy as someone else (2:19-22).

Almost no one doubts that Paul wrote it. Scholars of every kind, those who hold traditional views of the Bible and those who do not, count Philippians among the letters that are certainly his. The personal news, the style and the teaching all fit him.

The early church knew it too. Early in the second century Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, wrote his own letter to the church in Philippi, and in it he reminds them that Paul, when he was away from them, wrote them letters.

Timothy matters to the story. He had joined Paul shortly before the church in Philippi was founded (Acts 16:1-3), so the Philippians had known him from the first. Paul says of him, “I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs” (2:20).

parts.h: Philippi, and how the church began
parts.body:
Philippi lay in Macedonia, in what is now northern Greece, on a great Roman road that crossed the Balkans. It was named after Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great. In 42 BC, on the plain outside the city, Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, the men who had killed Julius Caesar. Soldiers who had fought there were settled in the city, and after Octavian's victory at Actium in 31 BC more settlers came, and Philippi became a Roman colony.

A colony was a small piece of Rome planted abroad. Its people were Roman citizens, governed by Roman law and Roman officials, and they were proud of it. That pride helps explain two things Paul says. He tells them, “conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ” (1:27), using a word that means to live as a citizen. And he says, “But our citizenship is in heaven” (3:20).

Acts tells how the church began, around AD 49 or 50 (Acts 16). Paul and his companions crossed by sea from Asia into Macedonia. On the Sabbath they went outside the city to a place of prayer by the river, and spoke to some women there. One of them, Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, believed and was baptized with her household, and she opened her home to them. Later Paul freed a slave girl from a spirit that told fortunes for her owners. Her owners had Paul and Silas beaten and thrown into prison. That night, as they sang hymns, an earthquake opened the doors, and the jailer and his household believed.

So the church began with a businesswoman, a slave girl and a jailer. And it never forgot Paul. When he left Macedonia, it alone supported him, and even while he was in Thessalonica it sent help more than once (4:15-16).

Paul is in chains (1:7, 13). He is waiting for a trial whose outcome he does not know: it could end in his release or in his death (1:20-25). But the letter does not say where he is, and Christians have answered in three ways. These notes do not choose.

The view held longest, and still by most, is Rome, where Acts says Paul lived under guard for two years, about AD 60 to 62 (Acts 28:30). Those who hold it point to ‘the whole palace guard’ (1:13), which fits the emperor's own guard in Rome, and to the greeting from ‘the household of Caesar’ (4:22). A trial before the emperor would also explain why Paul's life hangs in the balance.

A second view is Ephesus, in the mid-50s. Acts does not tell of a prison there, but Paul speaks of many imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:23) and of a deadly danger in the province of Asia. Ephesus is much closer to Philippi than Rome, which would make the several trips the letter implies easier: news of Paul's arrest reaching Philippi, Epaphroditus travelling to him, news of his illness reaching home, and his return.

A third view is Caesarea, where Paul was held for about two years, about AD 57 to 59, in Herod's palace (Acts 23:35). The word for ‘palace guard’ could also mean a governor's headquarters, and the ‘household of Caesar’ could mean the emperor's servants in any province.

Whichever it was, the message is the same. A man who may soon die writes to friends about joy.

parts.h: One letter, or more than one?
parts.body:
At 3:1 Paul writes, “Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord.” But the letter does not end there. Instead, in the next verse the tone turns sharp: “Watch out for those dogs” (3:2). And the thanks for the gift comes near the very end (4:10-20), not at the start where readers might expect it.

So some scholars think Philippians joins two or three shorter letters Paul sent to Philippi, perhaps including a short note of thanks for the gift. Many others think it is one letter. They point to words and themes that run through every part of it, and note that Paul often uses ‘finally’ to mark a turn rather than an end. These notes do not choose. On either view the whole letter is Paul's, and the church has always read it as one.

Greeting, thanks and prayer (1:1-11). Paul thanks God for the Philippians' partnership in the gospel from the first day, and prays that their love will grow in knowledge.

Paul's news (1:12-26). His chains have helped the gospel spread. Some preach Christ from rivalry, some from love, and Paul rejoices either way. He weighs life and death: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21).

A life worthy of the gospel (1:27 to 2:18). Stand together; be humble; look to others' interests. Then the song of Christ, who emptied himself and was exalted (2:5-11). So “work out your salvation”, for God is at work in you (2:12-13), and shine like lights.

Two friends (2:19-30). Timothy, whom Paul hopes to send soon, and Epaphroditus, who nearly died serving Paul and is now going home. Both live out the mind of Christ.

Knowing Christ (chapter 3). Paul warns against teachers who trusted in circumcision. He lists his own proud record as a Jew, and counts it all as loss compared with knowing Christ. He presses on toward the goal, and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven.

Last words (chapter 4). A plea to two women leaders to agree; rejoice, pray instead of worrying, think on what is good; Paul's thanks for their gift and his secret of contentment; greetings.

Notice how the song in chapter 2 shapes the rest. Timothy, Epaphroditus and Paul himself are each shown giving themselves for others, as Christ did.

“Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” (2:5). Then come six verses so carefully shaped that many scholars think they are an early Christian hymn Paul quotes, perhaps one the Philippians already sang. Others think Paul wrote them himself. Either way, they are among the most important words about Jesus in the whole Bible.

The song goes down, then up. Christ, “existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness” (2:6-7). He humbled himself further, “and became obedient to death— even death on a cross” (2:8). Crucifixion was the death Rome kept for slaves and rebels. Then God acts: “Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names” (2:9), so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess “that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (2:11).

The church confesses what this song says. Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. The Nicene Creed confesses him as ‘very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father’, who ‘came down from heaven’ and ‘was made man’. The Council of Chalcedon in AD 451 confessed him as one person, ‘truly God and truly man’, in two natures ‘without confusion, without change, without division, without separation’. These are not the site's views. They are the faith of the church, and the song in Philippians is one of the places that faith comes from.

What does ‘emptied Himself’ mean, then? Not that he stopped being God. The song explains the emptying by what he took on: the form of a servant, human likeness. He did not subtract God; he added man. He did not cling to the honour and rights that were his, but laid them aside to serve. And the end of the song gives him the worship Isaiah says belongs to the LORD alone, which would make no sense if he had ceased to be God.

Some teachers in the 1800s proposed that the Son gave up certain powers of God, such as knowing all things, in order to live a truly human life. Many who hold such ideas mean to keep the creeds, and Christians still discuss how the Son's divine and human life fit together. But any teaching that Christ stopped being God, or was only partly God while on earth, steps outside what the church confesses. The note on Philippians 2 says more.

Joy. Words for joy and rejoicing come more than a dozen times, written by a man in chains. Paul's joy does not rest on how things are going. It rests on the Lord, on the gospel spreading, and on his friends. It is joy that has looked at suffering and death and not been undone.

The mind of Christ. The letter keeps using a Greek verb that means to think, to set your mind, to have an attitude. “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” (2:5). Humility here is not thinking badly of yourself. It is using whatever you have for the good of others, as Christ did.

Partnership. Paul thanks them for their ‘partnership in the gospel’ (1:5). The Greek word, koinonia, means sharing a common life and a common cause. They prayed, they gave, they sent one of their own. The Christian life in this letter is shared work, not a private hobby.

Citizenship. In a city proud of being Roman, Paul tells believers to live as citizens worthy of the gospel, and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven. They still live in Philippi. But their first loyalty belongs to the Lord Jesus Christ.

The day of Christ. Paul looks ahead again and again to ‘the day of Christ’ (1:6, 10; 2:16), when the Lord will come and “transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (3:21). The hope of this letter is resurrection, not escape.

Philippians quotes the Old Testament less than some of Paul's letters, but it is full of it.

The song of Christ ends with words from Isaiah. There the LORD says, “Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance” (Isaiah 45:23). Paul says every knee will bow at the name of Jesus. He gives to Jesus the honour that Isaiah says belongs to Israel's God alone.

The song also sounds like Isaiah's servant, who “poured out His life unto death” and whom God would raise and exalt (Isaiah 53:12; 52:13).

When Paul says his troubles “will turn out for my deliverance” (1:19), his Greek words match the old Greek translation of Job 13:16, where Job trusts that God will vindicate him. When he warns against ‘complaining or arguing’ in ‘a crooked and perverse generation’ (2:14-15), he echoes Israel in the wilderness and the song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:5). And when he pictures his own death as a ‘drink offering’ poured out (2:17), he uses the language of Israel's worship (Numbers 28:7).

In chapter 3 Paul tells his own story as a Jew: circumcised on the eighth day, as God commanded Abraham (Genesis 17:12), of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee. He does not despise any of it. He says that compared with knowing Christ, even these good gifts are loss, and he boasts as Jeremiah said to boast: in knowing the Lord (Jeremiah 9:24).

It is not a promise of success or wealth. “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength” (4:13) is often printed on sports shirts and lifted out as a promise that God will help you win. In its place it says the opposite of what many hope. Paul has learned to be content “to being filled and being hungry, to having plenty and having need” (4:12). The strength Christ gives him is the strength to go hungry without despair. And “my God will supply all your needs” (4:19) is said to a generous church, about needs, not wants. Any teaching that turns these verses into a promise of health and wealth misreads a letter written in chains.

It is not a rebuke of anxious people. “Be anxious for nothing” (4:6) is an invitation to bring every worry to God in prayer, not a rule that faithful people never feel anxious. Paul himself speaks of being anxious for his friend (2:28). Nothing in the letter shames a worried person, or forbids getting medical help.

It is not contempt for the Jewish people. The hard words of 3:2 are aimed at teachers who said Gentile believers must be circumcised to belong to God's people, a dispute among believers in Jesus. Paul himself is a Jew and says so with care (3:5). The note on Acts 2:22-28 says why this site rejects any reading that turns the New Testament into contempt for Jews.

And it is not a call to put any nation first. ‘Our citizenship is in heaven’ (3:20) was written to people proud of being Roman. It asks believers in every country to hold their earthly loyalties loosely, under the Lord Jesus. The cross belongs to no flag.

Read it in one sitting, as a letter between friends. It is full of thanks, news, worry, love and requests, and it reads best that way.

Watch for the words that come back: joy and rejoicing, the gospel, partnership, the mind, the day of Christ.

Notice the song in chapter 2, and then notice how the rest of the letter lives it out. Timothy cares for others' interests. Epaphroditus risks his life. Paul counts his gains as loss. Christ's way down becomes their way of life.

Notice where the joy sits. It is not cheerfulness or pretending. It sits beside chains, rivalry, illness, quarrels and the chance of death. That is what makes it worth having.

When a line has become famous on its own, like 4:13, read the verses around it before you claim it.

And let the letter ask you its questions. Whose interests do you look after? What do you count as gain? What would it take for you to be content? And in whose hands is your life, whether you live or die?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘Overseers and deacons.’ What these leaders were, and why churches today read them differently.
‘To depart and be with Christ.’ What all Christians confess about death, and where they differ about the time before the resurrection.
‘He emptied Himself.’ Why this never meant Christ stopped being God, as the creeds confess.
‘Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.’ Not earning it: God's work and ours together.
‘Those dogs … those mutilators of the flesh.’ Whom Paul meant, and why this is no word against the Jewish people.
Faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? Two readings of one Greek phrase.
‘Be anxious for nothing.’ An invitation to prayer, not a rebuke of anxious people.
‘I can do all things.’ Contentment in hunger and in plenty, not a slogan for ambition.
‘My God will supply all your needs.’ Why this is not a promise of wealth.

words.line: Greek chara and chairō. Gladness rooted in the Lord, not in circumstances. “Rejoice in the Lord always” (4:4).
Greek koinonia, a shared life and common cause. The Philippians shared in Paul's work by prayer, gifts and help (1:5).
Greek phroneō, to think, set your mind, hold an attitude. “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” (2:5).

words.word: Form of God, form of a servant
words.line: Christ shared God's very nature, and took the nature of a servant as well (2:6-7). The same word ‘form’ is used of both.
Greek kenoō. Christ ‘emptied Himself’ by taking the form of a servant (2:7), not by ceasing to be God.
The name given to Jesus, the name Isaiah gives to Israel's God. Every tongue will confess “that Jesus Christ is Lord” (2:11).
Leaders of the church in Philippi (1:1). Overseer later became the word for bishop; deacon means servant.
Greek politeuma, the state you belong to. In a Roman colony Paul says “our citizenship is in heaven” (3:20).
Words from bookkeeping. Paul moves everything he was proud of into the loss column, for the sake of Christ (3:7-8).
Greek autarkēs, a word the Stoic teachers prized. Paul's contentment comes from Christ who strengthens him (4:11-13).
The day Christ returns, when his work in his people is finished (1:6) and their bodies are made new (3:21).
